title: Should Christians Support the Death Penalty?
excerpt: Genesis 9:6 grounds the penalty for murder in the image of God, and the murderer bears that image too. The case for the state's sword and the case against it are both as old as the church, and each has a question it would rather not be asked.
body:
A mother sits through the trial of the man who killed her son, and on the last day someone from her church squeezes her hand and says she will be praying that the mother can forgive. A chaplain has spent four years visiting a condemned man who was baptized in a prison sink, and he no longer knows what he thinks justice requires. A retired man who never doubted that murderers should die read one morning about a prisoner released after decades because the evidence had been wrong, and he hasn't been able to settle the matter in his mind since.

The skeptic sees a contradiction either way. Christians say every human life is sacred, and a great many of them want the state to take some. Other Christians say the state must never kill, and their own Bible commands it in more than one place. He asks which of them has read the book.

Some people come to this question carrying a death. For them the argument is not the first thing. If you're grieving as you read this, you don't have to resolve any of it before you're allowed to pray. Bring the question to God in whatever words you have; the psalms give you permission. Bring it to a person too, a friend or a pastor who will sit with you. If you have started to wonder whether you want to go on living, reach out today: in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This essay can't counsel you, but [Find Help](/help) has other lines you can call and a page for grief.

What follows is not legal advice, and it names no court and no case. It is about what Scripture says and what Christians have made of it.

## The Verse Given to Noah

The oldest text is spoken to Noah after the flood, before there was an Israel or a law of Moses. "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image" (Genesis 9:6).

The reason given is the remarkable part. Murder is answered with death because the victim bore the image of God. To kill a human being is to strike at the one whose likeness he carried, and the penalty is a measure of what was destroyed. Those who support capital punishment have always started here, and they point out that a command given to Noah is given to the ancestor of every nation and not to one people for one period.

Those who oppose it start in the same sentence. The murderer is also made in the image of God, and nothing he has done has removed it. Some read the verse as a statement of what violence brings on itself, closer to a proverb than a statute. Others note that a few pages earlier God dealt with the first murderer himself, and he marked Cain so that no one would kill him (Genesis 4:15). The Study Bible's note on [Genesis 9](/study/bible/genesis/9) sets out both readings and says plainly, "Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it."

## The Law of Moses

The law given at Sinai required death for murder, "Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death" (Exodus 21:12), and it refused to let a rich killer buy his way out: "you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer" (Numbers 35:31). It gave the reason in terms of the land itself, which blood pollutes, so that "no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it" (Numbers 35:33).

Two things about that law complicate any simple appeal to it. The first is its range. It prescribed death for adultery (Leviticus 20:10), for cursing a parent (Exodus 21:17), for breaking the Sabbath (Exodus 31:14) and for a good deal else. Whoever appeals to Moses for the murderer has to explain why he does not appeal to Moses for the rest, and one answer, that Israel's civil code was for Israel, puts the weight back on Genesis.

The second is its caution. No one could be executed on the word of one witness: "On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death" (Deuteronomy 17:6). The witnesses had to throw the first stones themselves (Deuteronomy 17:7). A witness who lied in a capital case was to receive the penalty he had tried to bring on the accused (Deuteronomy 19:18-19). And over the whole system stood a warning to the judges: "do not kill the innocent and righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked" (Exodus 23:7). The law that commanded execution was more afraid of executing the wrong person than many later Christian governments were.

There is also what God himself did. David committed adultery and arranged a murder, and the law demanded his life twice over. When he confessed, the prophet told him, "The Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die" (2 Samuel 12:13). The God who gave the penalty said of himself, "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11).

## The Sword in Romans 13

The chief New Testament text is Paul's. The ruler, he writes, "is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:4).

It should be read with the sentence that comes a few lines before it. "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God" (Romans 12:19). Paul takes vengeance out of the hands of the injured person, and then he says where a part of it has been placed. The Study Bible's note on Romans 13 explains that the sword was the emblem of a magistrate's power to punish, and that this power included execution. Paul does not seem troubled by it. On trial for his own life he said, "If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death" (Acts 25:11). He assumed there were such things.

What the passage does not say is that every use of the sword is just. Paul wrote it under an empire that had crucified his Lord on a false charge and that, by the church's memory, later put him to death. He describes what government is for. He gives no promise that it will do it.

## The Woman and the Stones

The story most often quoted against the death penalty is in John 8. A note is needed first: as the Study Bible explains, the passage is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts, and the ESV prints it in double brackets. It has been read in the church for many centuries, and both sides appeal to it.

Men bring Jesus a woman taken in adultery and remind him that Moses commanded stoning. He answers, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her" (John 8:7). They leave one at a time. To the woman he says, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more" (John 8:11).

Opponents of capital punishment hear a principle in this. Jesus does not say the law was wrong. He asks who is fit to carry it out, and nobody is. Supporters answer that the scene is a trap set by a mob and not a trial. The man caught with her is missing, no court has sat, and the witnesses are using a human being as bait. On their reading Jesus breaks up a lynching and says nothing about what a lawful judge may do. Both readings are possible. The story itself settles only that the one person there who was without sin did not want her dead.

## The Case For

Through most of the church's history most of its major teachers have held that the state may put a murderer to death, and their case was never mere bloodlust. It rests on retribution, which is a different thing from revenge. Revenge is what the injured do in their own cause. Retribution is a public judgment that a wrong was done and that it deserves an answer in proportion. To say that no crime could ever forfeit the criminal's life, on this view, is to say that the victim's life was worth less than Scripture says it was.

Augustine, in the fifth century, wrote that the commandment against killing has exceptions made by God's own authority, and that an official who carries out a lawful sentence "is but the sword in the hand of him who uses it." Thomas Aquinas compared the dangerous offender to a diseased limb: if a man is "dangerous and infectious to the community," it is right that he be killed "in order to safeguard the common good." John Calvin answered those who thought a Christian magistrate should never shed blood: God binds the hands of private men, he wrote, but "he does not bind his own justice, which he exercises by the hands of magistrates." The Westminster Confession says that God has armed rulers "with the power of the sword, for the defense and encouragement of them that are good, and for the punishment of evil-doers," and the articles of the English church say that the law "may punish Christian men with death, for heinous and grievous offences."

What this side fears is a mercy paid for by someone else. A society that will not say that the worst crimes deserve the gravest penalty has, they think, quietly told the murdered and their families that what was taken from them was not so very great.

## The Case Against

The other case is just as old. In the second century the Christian writer Athenagoras, defending the church against the rumor that it practiced murder, told the emperor, "we cannot endure even to see a man put to death, though justly." Tertullian, around the year 200, thought a Christian could hold public office only if he could manage it without "sitting in judgment on any one's life." The Anabaptists of 1527 put it into a confession: the sword "is ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ." The state may wield it, they said, and a disciple may not.

Even among those who granted the state its right, there is a long record of asking it not to use it. In 412 several men confessed to murdering one priest and maiming another, and Augustine, the same Augustine quoted above, wrote to the judge. "Our desire," he said, "is rather that justice be satisfied without the taking of their lives or the maiming of their bodies in any part." He did not ask for the men to go free. He asked that they be restrained and given time: "Fulfil, Christian judge, the duty of an affectionate father." His reason was the offenders' souls. A dead man cannot repent.

To this the modern argument adds two things. One is error. The Bible's own safeguards assume that courts can convict the innocent, and in our own time people who had been sentenced to die have been cleared and released. A prisoner wrongly held can be let go, and one wrongly executed cannot. The penalty has also tended to fall more heavily on the poor and the despised than on those who could pay for a defense. The other is that a modern state can hold a dangerous man securely for life, which Noah's world could not. In 2018 the catechism of the Catholic Church, which had long allowed the penalty, was revised to say that "the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person."

What this side fears is the state claiming a finality that belongs to God, and using it on someone God had not finished with.

## A Hard Question for Each

Each case has a question it tends to avoid.

The supporter is asked about the safeguards. If Genesis 9 binds every government, does Deuteronomy's standard of proof bind it too? Moses required two eyewitnesses and made them the executioners. Many modern convictions would not meet that test, and a Christian who wants Moses' penalty should say whether he also wants Moses' caution. He is also asked what he will say to the family of the first innocent person killed.

The opponent is asked about the blood. Scripture says that Abel's blood cried out from the ground (Genesis 4:10), and it does not treat that cry as something to be talked out of. If execution is always wrong, was it wrong when God commanded it? One answer is that the penalty was just in principle and has become unnecessary and too dangerous in practice. That is a serious answer, and it concedes that the argument is about prudence and not about whether the murderer deserves it.

## What We Have Done with It

The church's own record should make both sides slower. For centuries we handed over people to be killed for crimes that were not crimes at all. We burned heretics. The history course on this site records the Protestant city that burned a man as a heretic and the church courts that were authorized to use torture, and Christians on every side drowned and hanged each other during the Reformation in God's name. A church with that history is in no position to speak of the state's sword as though it had always been in safe hands.

We have failed in the other direction too. Churches that speak warmly of mercy for the offender have often had nothing to say to the people he bereaved, and have left them, as one page on this site puts it, "alone with a pain the church declined to take seriously." It is possible to visit the prisoner and never once call the widow.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Some things are settled. Murder is an attack on the image of God. The state has real authority to punish, and private vengeance is forbidden to a Christian. No court may kill the innocent, and a system careless about that stands under the warning of Exodus. The condemned person remains a human being to whom the gospel is offered until his last breath. And no Christian may take pleasure in an execution, because God does not.

Whether the state should put murderers to death now is not settled among faithful Christians. It is not a question the creeds decide. The best of the church's teachers stand on both sides of it, and this essay takes no side.

To the mother in the courtroom, neither answer says what she is supposed to feel. Her anger is no sin. It is very close to what God said he heard from the ground. Nobody has the right to give her a date by which she must have forgiven. Paul's sentence about vengeance doesn't tell her the wrong was small. It tells her that it will be repaid, and by whom.

On the day Jesus died the state executed three men. One of them said of himself and the other, "we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong" (Luke 23:41). He asked to be remembered, and he was told, "today you will be with me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). Jesus did not take him down from the cross. The man was forgiven and he died that afternoon under his sentence. Both sides of this argument can find their case in him, and neither can get past the third cross, where an innocent man was tried, sentenced and killed.

*"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image."* (Genesis 9:6)

*"I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live."* (Ezekiel 33:11)
